title: Bailis-2015-CoordinationAvoidanceInDistributedDatabases-Thesis
universal_lens: Coordination avoidance formalizes minimal synchronization constraints in distributed systems through semantic alignment of application integrity and data consistency. Invariant confluence formalizes coordination avoidance through global validity of local commit decisions, enabling precise characterization of when distributed systems can operate without inter-replica synchronization.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian inference models application-level integrity constraints as probabilistic distributions over system states, enabling conformal prediction of coordination costs. Bayesian inference over invariant-confluent histories enables probabilistic tracking of correctness violations, supporting adaptive risk-aware transaction scheduling in GSI.
gse_mapping: Situationally grounded reasoning maps semantic data dependencies to state transitions in distributed partitions, optimizing for latency-constrained integrity guarantees. Situational reasoning in GSE leverages invariant confluence to model state transitions where local actions remain consistent under global invariants, enabling dynamic coordination-free execution paths.

primitives.name: Coordination Cost Function
primitives.verbatim_quote: Given the availability, latency, and throughput penalties associated with classic mechanisms such as serializable transactions, a broad class of systems (e.g., "NoSQL") has sought weaker alternatives that reduce the use of expensive coordination during system operation, often at the cost of application integrity.
primitives.assumptions: Classic coordination mechanisms impose linear overhead in latency and throughput; weaker models trade integrity for efficiency.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When L > threshold or A < acceptable bound, coordination avoidance becomes necessary.

layer2.mapping: Maps semantic integrity requirements to empirical coordination cost metrics in distributed data systems.
layer2.telemetry: Latency, throughput, and availability measurements under varying coordination levels.

primitives.name: Read Committed Isolation
primitives.verbatim_quote: As a simple example, consider the common Read Committed (RC) isolation guarantee [9], which is the default semantics in fifteen of eighteen popular relational databases, including Oracle, SAP Hana, and Microsoft SQL Server (Chapter 4). Informally, Read Committed ensures that users never read non-final writes to data; if, within a transaction, a user sets her username to "Sally" and, subsequently, sets her username to "Sal," no other user should ever read that the user's username is "Sally."
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'RC': 'Read Committed isolation level (dimensionless)', 'W_i': 'write operation i (timestamped)', 'R_j': 'read operation j (timestamped)', 'T': 'transaction time (ms)'}
primitives.assumptions: RC prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads; requires timestamp-based ordering of operations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When concurrent reads occur before final writes, RC may yield inconsistent views.

layer2.mapping: RC semantics map to temporal consistency kernels in distributed state machines.
layer2.telemetry: Timestamp consistency checks and read-write conflict resolution logs.

primitives.name: Invariant Confluence Condition
primitives.verbatim_quote: DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS 33 3.3 Discussion and Limitations Invariant Confluence captures a simple, informal rule: coordination can only be avoided if all local commit decisions are globally valid.

primitives.name: Commit Decision Composability

primitives.name: Unsafe Execution Detection

primitives.name: Read-Subset-Items-Written Property
primitives.verbatim_quote: A read-only transaction Tr exhibits the ReadSubset-Items-Written property if, whenever Tr reads a version produced by a write-only transaction Tw, Tr only reads items written to by Tw.
primitives.assumptions: Transactions are categorized as read-only or write-only; reads are constrained to subsets of writes.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When Tr reads V_tw, Tr's read set ⊆ Tw's write set.

layer2.mapping: RSIW ensures that read-only transactions observe only what was explicitly written by a corresponding write-only transaction, enabling a formal isomorphism between causal consistency and one-copy serializability.
layer2.telemetry: Verification of read set inclusion within write set across transaction pairs.

primitives.name: One-Copy Serializable History
primitives.verbatim_quote: A history is one-copy serializable if it is view equivalent to a serial execution of the transactions over a single logical copy of the database.
primitives.assumptions: View equivalence holds between concurrent and serial histories.
primitives.breakdown_regime: View equivalence implies identical read and write behaviors under serial execution.

layer2.mapping: Derived from view equivalence, this kernel enables formal verification of consistency in distributed databases without requiring global coordination.
layer2.telemetry: Comparison of read/write views between concurrent and serial histories.

primitives.name: RA Isolation Equivalence
primitives.verbatim_quote: That is, for read-only and write-only transactions, if each reading transaction only reads a subset of the items that another write-only transaction wrote, then RA isolation is equivalent to one-copy serializable isolation.
primitives.assumptions: Read-only and write-only transaction types exist; subset constraint applies to item access.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Equivalence holds when read sets are subsets of write sets.

layer2.mapping: RA isolation is formally isomorphic to OCS when transaction access patterns satisfy subset constraints, enabling equivalence in consistency guarantees.
layer2.telemetry: Validation of subset containment between read and write sets in transaction pairs.

primitives.name: RAMP Protocol State Transition
primitives.verbatim_quote: If a history H containing read-only and write-only transactions has RSIW and is valid under RA isolation, then H is one-copy serializable.
primitives.assumptions: History contains only read-only and write-only transactions; RSIW property holds; RA isolation is enforced.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Transition from RA-isolated history to one-copy serializable form occurs under RSIW.

layer2.mapping: The derived kernel shows how RSIW and RA isolation jointly ensure that histories maintain one-copy serializability through state transition logic.
layer2.telemetry: Tracking of state transitions in transaction histories under RA and RSIW constraints.

reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 1 of Bailis' thesis introduces the foundational problem of coordination avoidance in distributed databases. It establishes that modern internet-scale systems face a trade-off between data consistency and operational efficiency. The core thesis is that by understanding and leveraging application semantics, it is possible to reduce or eliminate unnecessary coordination. This is achieved through formalizing the notion of 'minimal coordination'—whereby systems only coordinate when absolutely required to maintain integrity. The chapter outlines how classical approaches like serializable transactions incur significant latency and throughput penalties due to locking and consensus protocols. In contrast, newer systems adopt weaker consistency models that allow for greater concurrency and performance. The key insight is that these systems do not abandon integrity but rather shift its definition based on application needs. For instance, Read Committed isolation is shown to be sufficient for many applications, allowing for lock-free implementations. The chapter also highlights the importance of separating visibility from progress, which enables composability of operations. This separation is critical for designing systems where multiple clients interact with shared data without requiring full coordination. The mathematical framing involves defining coordination cost functions that quantify the trade-offs between consistency and performance. These functions are used to derive optimal strategies for avoiding unnecessary coordination while preserving semantic integrity. The chapter further discusses how this approach applies to various domains such as data serving, transaction processing, and web services. Each domain presents unique challenges in terms of how to encode semantic requirements into system behavior. For example, in transaction processing, the goal is to ensure atomicity and durability while minimizing coordination overhead. In web services, the challenge lies in maintaining consistency across heterogeneous components. Overall, the chapter sets up the theoretical framework for analyzing and implementing coordination avoidance techniques, laying the groundwork for subsequent chapters that explore specific algorithmic solutions.
